title: The 52-Week Savings Challenge That Fits a Small Paycheck
description: The 52-week savings challenge for small paychecks: classic, reverse, flat, half and bingo versions, plus how to pre-fund the hard December weeks.

cover.alt: A glass jar full of coins next to a small blank desk calendar

keywords: 52 week savings challenge 52 week money challenge reverse 52 week challenge savings challenge printable
takeaways: The classic challenge saves $1,378: $1 in week one, rising to $52 in week 52.
The last weeks are the hardest, so pick a version that fits your pay, or pre-fund December.
The half version still saves $689, enough for a $400 emergency.
body:
You have probably seen the chart. Save $1 in week one, $2 in week two, and keep adding a dollar a week until you reach $52 in week 52. Finish all 52 weeks and you have $1,378. It looks painless, and for the first few months it honestly is. Here is the part most pages about the 52 week savings challenge skip. The plan is back loaded. The cheap weeks come first, and the expensive weeks land at the end of the year, in November and December, when money is already tight for almost everyone. If your paycheck is small, that design flaw is usually why the challenge dies somewhere around week 44. The fix is not more willpower. It is choosing the version of the challenge that fits your pay. Below you will find the classic version, plus four others: the reverse, the flat, the half, and a pick any week bingo style. They all build the same habit. They just ask for the money at different times. It is a habit worth building. In the Federal Reserve's Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, fielded in October 2025, only 63 percent of adults in the US said they would cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent. A finished challenge gives you $1,378, which covers an expense that size more than three times over. ## How the Classic Challenge Works Bank of America and SoFi describe the classic version the same way, because there is only one rule. In week one you move $1 into savings. In week two, $2. Every week the deposit grows by $1, and in week 52 you deposit $52. Added together, the deposits come to $1,378. The early weeks feel almost too easy, which is the whole appeal. By the end of week 13 you have saved $91 without ever putting aside more than $13 at a time. The habit forms before the amounts get serious. | Week | That week's deposit | Total saved so far | |------|---------------------|--------------------| | 1 | $1 | $1 | | 4 | $4 | $10 | | 13 | $13 | $91 | | 26 | $26 | $351 | | 39 | $39 | $780 | | 52 | $52 | $1,378 | For many people this challenge is the start of an emergency fund. If that is your goal, it helps to read [how to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) alongside this one, so you know what size cushion you are aiming for. ## The Honest Problem With the Classic Version Now look at that table from the other end. The first 13 weeks of the classic challenge cost $91 in total. The last 13 weeks cost $598. Weeks 49 to 52 alone ask for $49, $50, $51, and $52, which is $202 across four weeks. If you started in January, those are the four weeks running into the end of December. That timing is rough. December is when heating bills rise, holiday spending happens, and hours at seasonal jobs can get cut. A plan that demands its biggest payments in the most expensive month of the year is a plan built to be abandoned. Most people do not quit the classic challenge because they are bad at saving. They quit because week 48 collides with real life. Every version below fixes that collision in a different way. ## Four Versions That Fit a Real Paycheck ### The Reverse Version: Start at $52, End at $1 Deposit $52 in week one, then $1 less each week, finishing with $1 in week 52. The total is still $1,378, because it is the same 52 amounts in the opposite order. By the end of week 13 you already have $598 saved, which feels great and makes the challenge much harder to walk away from. Your weekly deposit shrinks all year, and by December you are putting aside $4, $3, $2, and $1. SoFi suggests this order for exactly that reason: the biggest deposits happen while the challenge is new and motivation is high, not during the holidays. The catch is the start. Finding $52 in week one and $51 in week two is a real ask on a small paycheck. The reverse version suits people whose January is quieter than their December, or who get a tax refund, a bonus, or a run of extra shifts early in the year that can carry the heavy weeks. ### The Flat Version: $26.50 Every Week Save $26.50 every week for 52 weeks. No ladder, no chart, no thinking. The math: $26.50 times 52 weeks is $1,378, the same total as the classic version. This is the easiest version to automate, because a standing weekly transfer of $26.50 never changes. It also matches a steady paycheck well, since every week costs the same. The trade off is that there is no gentle warm up. Week one costs $26.50, the same as week 52, so the first month feels harder than the classic version's first month. If $26.50 is too much right now, the half version below uses the same steady idea at $13.25 a week, which totals $689. ### The Half Version: Same Ladder, Half the Money Run the classic ladder at half size. Save 50 cents in week one, $1 in week two, and add 50 cents a week until you reach $26 in week 52. Your biggest single deposit all year is $26, and the total is $689. Half the money might sound like a failed challenge. It is not. Measured against that Federal Reserve survey, $689 still covers a $400 emergency with room to spare, and it does it on deposits a tight budget can actually carry. Finishing the half version beats starting the classic one three times and quitting in November each time. You can always run it a second time, or step up to a bigger version, once the habit is in place. ### The Bingo Version: Pick Any Week Write the numbers 1 to 52 on a chart, in any order. Each week, look at your money first, then pick one number you can afford and cross it off. Good week, overtime paid out, a side job came through? Cross off $47. Bad week, the car needed a repair? Cross off $3 and move on. Cross off every number and you finish with $1,378. This version was made for irregular pay. If your hours change every week, a fixed ladder keeps landing on the wrong weeks, and this one bends instead. It pairs well with the approach in [how to budget with irregular income](/blog/budget-with-irregular-income/). One rule keeps bingo honest: try to clear at least one number above $40 in any month where money is decent. If you only ever pick the small numbers, you will reach December owing yourself a wall of $40 and $50 weeks, which is the classic problem all over again. | Version | Weekly deposit | Hardest single week | Total after 52 weeks | |---------|-----------------------|---------------------|----------------------| | Classic | $1 rising to $52 | $52, in week 52 | $1,378 | | Reverse | $52 falling to $1 | $52, in week 1 | $1,378 | | Flat | $26.50 every week | $26.50 | $1,378 | | Half | $0.50 rising to $26 | $26, in week 52 | $689 | | Bingo | You pick, $1 to $52 | Up to you | $1,378 | ## The Hard Months, and How to Pre-Fund Them Whichever version you pick, some months will be tighter than others. Rent increases, annual insurance bills, back to school costs, and December catch almost everyone. The trick is to see them coming and pay for them early, while your cheap weeks are running. Here is an illustration with made up numbers to show how pre-funding works. Say you start the classic challenge in January. Your December deposits, weeks 49 to 52, will cost $202 in total. If you add an extra $10 a week during your first 20 weeks, you set aside $200 before summer, and December is almost fully paid for before it arrives. SoFi makes the same point from the other side: paying ahead lets you skip or shrink deposits in a month you know will be tight. That is really just a small sinking fund for your own challenge, and the idea is explained in [sinking funds for beginners](/blog/sinking-funds-for-beginners/). You do not need a complicated system to keep track of all this. A simple spreadsheet where you tick off each week and watch the running total grow does the job, and we made a free one you can download and use as it is:

Download the free 52-Week Savings Challenge Tracker (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The Classic tab of the 52-week savings challenge tracker, with week dates, amounts, a Saved column and the running total](/assets/img/posts/52-week-savings-challenge-preview-1080x870.webp) It covers every version in the table above, so you can switch the amounts if your pay changes partway through the year. ## Where to Keep the Money While You Save Keep the challenge money in a savings account that is separate from the checking account your debit card pulls from. Money sitting in checking gets spent by accident. Money in a separate account has a small wall around it, and that wall is the whole point. SoFi makes two practical points here. First, a bank account beats an envelope or a jar, because the money can earn interest and is not sitting around your home. Second, an account with no debit card attached makes it harder to dip in on a weak day. You do not need anything fancy. A basic savings account at your current bank works fine. If your bank offers a high yield savings account, the interest adds a little extra over the year, and [what a high-yield savings account is](/blog/high-yield-savings-account/) explains how those accounts work. One small trick: name the account if your bank allows it. An account called Car Repairs or Holiday Fund is much harder to raid than one called Savings 2. ## When You Miss a Week (You Probably Will) It will happen. A bill lands wrong, hours get cut, something breaks. Missing a week is a normal part of this challenge, not the end of it. You have three decent options. Swap the missed amount with a smaller week still ahead of you, which is what the bingo version does by design. Split the missed deposit across the next two or three weeks. Or simply add a week at the end and finish at week 53. All three keep the habit alive, and the habit matters more than a perfect streak. What does not work is doubling up next week to punish yourself back onto the schedule. That turns one hard week into two, and it is how people talk themselves into quitting at $600 saved, which is a shame, because $600 is already a solid result. ## Frequently asked questions ### How much do you save with the 52 week savings challenge? The classic, reverse, flat, and bingo versions all total $1,378 over 52 weeks. The half version totals $689. Any interest your savings account pays comes on top of those numbers. ### When is the best time to start? Any week you like. January is traditional because New Year motivation is real, but the challenge is just 52 weeks in a row. Starting in March means finishing next March, and that is fine. If you can, pick a start date that lands just after a payday. ### I get paid every two weeks. Can I still do it? Yes. Combine two weeks into each paycheck. On the flat version that is $53 from each of 26 paychecks, which still adds up to $1,378. On the classic ladder, your first paycheck covers weeks one and two, $3 in total, and the amounts grow from there. ### Can I do the challenge in pounds or another currency? Yes. The math does not care about the currency. Save one unit in week one and follow the same ladder, and you end with 1,378 of whatever currency you are using. ### Should I do this challenge if I have credit card debt? A small savings cushion usually comes first, because without one, the next surprise expense goes straight back onto the card. Build a starter cushion with the half version, then put your extra money toward the debt. [How to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/) shows how to plan that payoff. ### Is the half version even worth doing? Yes. $689 covers a $400 emergency expense with money left over, and finishing a smaller challenge builds the weekly habit you need for bigger goals later. ## A quick note This article is general information for education only. It is not financial advice, and it does not take your income, debts, or tax situation into account. Savings account rates and terms change often, so check the current details with your bank before opening an account. ## Sources - [Bank of America, Better Money Habits, Money Saving Challenges That Will Teach You How to Successfully Save Money (updated October 2026).](https://bettermoneyhabits.bankofamerica.com/en/saving-budgeting/money-saving-challenges) - [SoFi Learn, 52-Week Savings Challenge (May 2026).](https://www.sofi.com/learn/content/52-week-savings-challenge/) - [Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025, Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (fielded October 2025).](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20260513a.htm)
